prompt: What runs a mapping data flow?
hint: Nobody writes its code.

choices.text: The copy activity's integration runtime, row by row
choices.why: A copy does not transform; a data flow runs as a Spark job.

choices.text: A Spark cluster the runtime starts
choices.why: Right. The boxes are turned into Spark by the service.

choices.text: The database it writes to, as stored procedures
choices.why: Nothing is pushed into the sink as procedures.

choices.text: Power Query, inside the factory
choices.why: That is Fabric's Dataflow Gen2, a different thing.

prompt: A team moving from Data Factory to Fabric plans to bring its mapping data flows across as Dataflow Gen2. What should it expect?
hint: Similar boxes, different engine.

choices.text: An import button that converts each data flow as it is
choices.why: Dataflow Gen2 is Power Query; there is no like-for-like conversion.

choices.text: To rebuild them in Power Query
choices.why: Right. Pipelines move more easily than data flows.

choices.text: Nothing to change, since both run on the same Spark
choices.why: Dataflow Gen2 does not run mapping data flow scripts.

choices.text: To keep them in Data Factory, since Fabric has no transformations
choices.why: Fabric has notebooks and Dataflow Gen2.

prompt: Which data flow box keeps one row per order when the shop resent some of them?
hint: Grouping by the order's id.

choices.text: Derived column
choices.why: It computes columns; it does not merge rows.

choices.text: Aggregate, grouped by the order
choices.why: Right. One group per order, keeping the first of each.

choices.text: Conditional split
choices.why: It sends rows down different paths; duplicates go down the same one.

choices.text: Alter row, set to delete
choices.why: Alter row marks rows for a database sink; it does not find duplicates.

prompt: Which of these does a notebook give that a mapping data flow does not? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think of what a program has.

choices.text: Rules that can be tested on four rows, on a laptop
choices.why: Yes, as `test_clean.py` does.

choices.text: Any library the cluster can install
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: A diff written by a person, reviewed line by line
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: A cluster that nobody has to choose or size
choices.why: That is the data flow's advantage; a notebook runs on a pool or cluster somebody picked.

choices.text: Running on Spark
choices.why: Both run on Spark.

prompt: An analyst commits yesterday's notebook to Git with its cell outputs. What is the risk?
hint: What do the outputs show?

choices.text: The notebook stops running, since outputs are read-only
choices.why: Outputs do not stop a notebook from running.

choices.text: Git refuses files larger than one cell
choices.why: Git takes the file; that is the problem.

choices.text: Rows of data, perhaps customers', are now in the repository
choices.why: Right. Clearing outputs before committing is the habit that prevents it.

choices.text: Spark reruns the outputs instead of the code at night
choices.why: A job runs the code; outputs are just text in the file.

prompt: A notebook cleans the night perfectly when its author runs the cells by hand, in order, choosing the date in the second cell. What makes it a job that can run at three in the morning?
hint: Who chooses the date at three in the morning?

choices.text: Running it on a larger cluster
choices.why: Size does not choose a date.

choices.text: A date parameter in the first cell
choices.why: Right. The same contract as the pipeline parameter `day` in lesson 19.

choices.text: Converting it into a mapping data flow
choices.why: A data flow needs the same parameter; converting adds nothing here.

choices.text: Saving its outputs, so that the job can reuse them
choices.why: A job runs the code again; old outputs are yesterday's.

prompt: Why does `clean.py` read every column of the export as text?
hint: Look at how the shop writes a total.

choices.text: Its totals, like `42,87`, are not numbers yet
choices.why: Right. The query turns text into types by rules the code states.

choices.text: Because the Parquet file it writes stores every column only as text
choices.why: Parquet stores types; the result has integers.

choices.text: DuckDB cannot read numbers out of a CSV file at all
choices.why: It can; the point is this CSV's numbers.

choices.text: Azurite returns blobs as strings
choices.why: It returns bytes.

prompt: The night's export had 2,972 rows and `clean.py` wrote 2,921 orders. How many rows were duplicates?
hint: Subtract.

prompt: `clean.py` was run twice for the same day, and `curated` still holds one file. What made the second run harmless?
hint: Where does it write, and how?

choices.text: DuckDB's `DISTINCT ON`, which removes the first run's rows
choices.why: It removes duplicates within one run's input; it never sees the first run's output.

choices.text: It writes to a fixed name for the day, replacing what is there
choices.why: Right. `overwrite=True` on one name per day.

choices.text: Azurite refuses a second blob in the same folder
choices.why: A container holds any number of blobs under one prefix.

choices.text: The export was deleted after the first run
choices.why: The second run read it again.

prompt: `clean.py` stores each total as an integer number of ___, the only safe way to keep money.
hint: A hundredth of a real.

prompt: Removing the comma from `42,87` instead of turning it into a point gives the right total for every row of the real export. Which row of the test catches it?
hint: Which total has one decimal digit?

choices.text: `42,87`, which becomes 4287 cents either way
choices.why: Exactly: two digits hide the mistake.

choices.text: `9,5`, which becomes 95 reais instead of 9.50
choices.why: Right. The shop always writes two digits, so only a test with one finds it.

choices.text: The order sent twice
choices.why: That row tests deduplication.

choices.text: None of them, since the test checks only the order ids
choices.why: It checks four rules, the totals among them.

prompt: What does a data flow's debug session give, and what does it not?
hint: Looking is not checking.

choices.text: A test suite that reruns on every change, at no cost
choices.why: It reruns nothing on its own, and the cluster is billed.

choices.text: Row previews; never a check that fails a change
choices.why: Right. Good for looking at data, and billed while it runs.

choices.text: Nothing; debug only shows the script
choices.why: It shows rows after each box.

choices.text: A local copy of the data flow for a laptop
choices.why: There is no local run of a data flow.

prompt: A team writes notebooks, and still cannot test them. Their notebook reads the raw files, cleans and writes in one long cell. What should change?
hint: Look at how `clean.py` is cut.

choices.text: Move to mapping data flows, which test themselves
choices.why: They do not; testing them needs a cluster.

choices.text: Run the cell twice and compare the outputs
choices.why: That checks repeatability, not the rules.

choices.text: Add more comments to the cell
choices.why: Comments check nothing.

choices.text: Put the rules in functions and keep storage at the edge
choices.why: Right. Then the rules can be fed four rows with no storage.

prompt: What does `time_to_live_min = 10` on the data flows runtime do?
hint: It is about the cluster after a run.

choices.text: Keeps the cluster, billed, for ten minutes after a run
choices.why: Right. The idle minutes are billed at the same rate as the work.

choices.text: Stops any data flow that is still running after ten minutes
choices.why: That would be a timeout; this is the opposite.

choices.text: Starts the cluster ten minutes before the trigger
choices.why: Nothing starts a cluster ahead of time.

choices.text: Deletes the data flow's output after ten minutes
choices.why: It concerns the cluster, not the data.

prompt: A data flow runs on 8 cores: a cold start the lesson takes as 5 minutes, then 3 minutes of work. How many vCore-hours is that run billed, to two decimals?
hint: Cores × minutes / 60.

prompt: Quitanda's night has two data flows, the second starting the moment the first ends. Why did ten minutes of time to live make it dearer?
hint: Compare what was saved with what was added.

choices.text: Time to live doubles the price per vCore-hour
choices.why: The rate is the same; the minutes changed.

choices.text: One start saved, ten idle minutes paid
choices.why: Right. 21 billed minutes against 16.

choices.text: A warm cluster works more slowly than a fresh one
choices.why: The work took three minutes in both arrangements.

choices.text: Both flows started their own cluster anyway
choices.why: The second found the first one's cluster warm.

prompt: The smallest cluster the provider accepts for a data flow runtime has ___ cores.
hint: The first number of the list `validate` printed.

prompt: A team of analysts who know SQL and Data Factory, and no Python, must join and aggregate tidy tables every night. What fits best?
hint: Who will look after it for three years?

choices.text: Mapping data flows
choices.why: Right. The people can build and change them, and the work is what the boxes do well.

choices.text: Notebooks, since code is always better
choices.why: Code nobody on the team can read is not better.

choices.text: A self-hosted integration runtime
choices.why: That is where a copy runs, not how a transformation is written.

choices.text: Fabric's Dataflow Gen2 inside Data Factory
choices.why: Dataflow Gen2 lives in Fabric, not in Data Factory.

prompt: Quitanda's night is about 3,000 rows. A colleague wants a Spark cluster for it from day one, "to be ready". What does the lesson's arithmetic say?
hint: How long did `clean.py` need, and how long does a cluster take to start?

choices.text: Spark is cheaper at every size, so start there
choices.why: At this size the start-up alone is more than the work.

choices.text: A cluster is needed for anything written to Parquet
choices.why: `clean.py` wrote Parquet from one process.

choices.text: At this size the cluster mostly starts, not works
choices.why: Right. Spark's moment is when the data stops fitting one machine or one night.

choices.text: Notebooks need Spark, so the choice is already made
choices.why: Fabric runs Python notebooks with no Spark session.

hint: Ask who maintains it, and what it needs.

pairs.left: SQL analysts, tidy tables, no Python
Rules that grow and need tests
pairs.right: A notebook with the rules in functions

pairs.left: An SSIS package written years ago

hint: Read, clean, write.
items: Keep one row per order and convert the payment and the total

prompt: Where would the rules of `clean.py` live if Quitanda chose a notebook in Fabric?
hint: The same Spark, written as code.

choices.text: In Fabric's Dataflow Gen2, which notebooks call
choices.why: Notebooks hold their own code.

choices.text: In the lakehouse's SQL analytics endpoint
choices.why: That endpoint is read-only, lesson 17.

choices.text: In the notebook's own functions, writing Delta
choices.why: Right. Same rules, read from `abfss://`, written as Delta.

choices.text: In a mapping data flow script stored beside the notebook
choices.why: Fabric has no mapping data flows.
